cards.title: Beyond quadratic lower bounds for general algebraic branching programs
cards.formal: What asymptotically stronger lower bound than the source’s quadratic benchmark can be proved for explicit polynomial families against general layered algebraic branching programs (ABPs)? An ABP over a field F computes a polynomial in commuting variables x₁,…,x_n by summing, over all paths from its source to its sink, the product of the affine linear labels on that path. Its size is the number of vertices. The intended lower bound must hold for every such ABP computing the chosen family, with no homogeneity, multilinearity, variable-order or width restriction on the ABP. The source does not state the new rate, degree regime, field or uniform explicitness requirement, so this remains an incomplete quantitative question.
cards.why: Stronger lower bounds for unrestricted ABPs would sharpen a central measure of algebraic computation between formulas and general circuits. The question concerns the cost of representing explicit polynomials despite sharing and cancellation.
cards.status_note: Read the conference definition and conclusion and the later author full version. Checked January 2026 multilinear status and the May revision notice for a claimed barrier; no matching unrestricted improvement was identified. The source still lacks a complete quantitative target.

sentences: Algebraic branching programs represent a polynomial as a sum of products along paths in a layered graph.
This question concerns the number of vertices when edge labels are arbitrary affine forms and no homogeneity restriction is imposed.
The source proves a tight quadratic bound for one power-sum family and asks for stronger lower bounds for explicit families.
It does not specify the desired rate, polynomial degrees, field or uniform construction requirement.
Those omissions remain visible, while separate multilinear results and a 2026 claim with an acknowledged gap are distinguished from progress on the general target.

cards.definitions: An ABP has finitely many layers V₀,…,V_ℓ, with V₀={s} and V_ℓ={t}, and edges directed only from V_j to V_{j+1}. Each edge e carries an affine form a_e,0+Σᵢa_e,i x_i with coefficients in F. A path weight is the formal polynomial product of its edge labels; the output is the sum of these products over all s-to-t paths, with equality as polynomials in F[x₁,…,x_n]. Labels may use all variables. Arbitrary field constants, repeated occurrences of variables and cancellation between paths are allowed. Define ABP_F(f) as the minimum Σ_j|V_j| over ABPs computing f. Counting edges or coefficient bits is a different measure. The polynomial’s total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient. An asymptotic family would consist of f_n in n variables, but both its degree bound and the algorithmic resource required to produce or access its coefficients still need to be specified. Merely choosing a polynomial of very large degree would introduce a depth lower bound unrelated to the intended improvement. The source’s example p_n=Σᵢx_i^n has ABP_F(p_n)=Θ(n²) when the field characteristic does not divide n, so a superquadratic bound cannot hold for this same family in this model.
cards.answer_criterion: A completed benchmark requires a fixed field convention, degree regime, explicit-family representation and resource bound, and a specified asymptotic lower-bound target. A result must then prove that every unrestricted layered ABP for the family has the required number of vertices. The present source passage does not determine those choices and therefore does not yet supply one complete acceptance predicate. A lower bound solely for homogeneous or multilinear ABPs, or solely for formulas, does not automatically establish the unrestricted claim.

context_blocks.title: What the quadratic result measures
context_blocks.text: The 2020 paper proves an Ω(n²) vertex lower bound for Σᵢx_i^n without assuming homogeneous ABPs. This matches a quadratic construction. It also treats degree-bounded polynomial edge labels, but the standard affine-label model is the baseline for this card.

context_blocks.title: A different question for unlayered graphs
context_blocks.text: The source separately asks for a nearly quadratic lower bound for unlayered ABPs computing the same power-sum polynomial. Unlayered programs and their edge measure are not the general layered-family improvement extracted here.

context_blocks.title: Why the quantitative choices matter
context_blocks.text: ABP variants simulate one another with polynomial overhead, but that overhead can erase a fixed polynomial improvement. This makes the vertex measure, affine labels and absence of homogeneity restrictions essential when comparing a proposed bound with the quadratic benchmark.

context_blocks.title: Later multilinear status
context_blocks.text: A January 2026 preprint reports that the best known lower bounds for multilinear ABPs remain quadratic and studies a limitation question for a particular lower-bound measure. This is adjacent evidence about a restricted model, not a stronger lower bound for the unrestricted ABPs of this card.

context_blocks.title: A claimed 2026 barrier has an acknowledged gap
context_blocks.text: A later preprint claimed an unconditional barrier for multilinear ABP lower bounds. Its 11 May 2026 revision notice reports a gap in Lemma 4.1 and says that all results depend on that lemma. The claim is therefore not recorded here as an established theorem.

cards.context:
The 2020 paper proves an Ω(n²) vertex lower bound for Σᵢx_i^n without assuming homogeneous ABPs. This matches a quadratic construction. It also treats degree-bounded polynomial edge labels, but the standard affine-label model is the baseline for this card.

The source separately asks for a nearly quadratic lower bound for unlayered ABPs computing the same power-sum polynomial. Unlayered programs and their edge measure are not the general layered-family improvement extracted here.

ABP variants simulate one another with polynomial overhead, but that overhead can erase a fixed polynomial improvement. This makes the vertex measure, affine labels and absence of homogeneity restrictions essential when comparing a proposed bound with the quadratic benchmark.

A January 2026 preprint reports that the best known lower bounds for multilinear ABPs remain quadratic and studies a limitation question for a particular lower-bound measure. This is adjacent evidence about a restricted model, not a stronger lower bound for the unrestricted ABPs of this card.

A later preprint claimed an unconditional barrier for multilinear ABP lower bounds. Its 11 May 2026 revision notice reports a gap in Lemma 4.1 and says that all results depend on that lemma. The claim is therefore not recorded here as an established theorem.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
